Luxury and Cash Fuel U.S. Housing Market
 
Plus, weak points in AI bonds and bracing for holiday travel
 
 
DAVID PAUL MORRIS/BLOOMBERG NEWS
 

America’s home-buying market is a house divided.

 

On one side, near-record home prices and the recent surge in mortgage rates above 7% have relegated buyers to the sidelines. In many cities, sales are stagnant and sellers are cutting prices for lower-end and entry-level homes to lure back buyers.

 

On the other is a robust luxury market, where wealthier home shoppers swerve around high rates with jumbo down payments or all-cash purchases. The top third of the market is still buying, and spending enough to push up home prices nationally by more than 4% over the past two years.

 

This dichotomy is playing out across the country.

 

Below, some of the best analysis and insight from WSJ writers and columnists, the Dow Jones Newswires team and occasionally beyond, on investing, the wealth-management business and more.

 
 
 

Planning & Investing

 

The Weak Points in AI Bonds Are Becoming Clearer

Market Talk

 

From Dow Jones Newswires

 

Inflationary pressures in Canada have yet to show any clear signs of broadening out despite persistently high energy prices, Desjardins’ Royce Mendes notes. Headline CPI inflation rose 0.1% on-month and 0.35% in seasonally-adjusted terms, taking the annual rate to 3.1%. Headline numbers were each a tick lower than expected by economists. Given the recent slowdown in the economy the Bank of Canada may still be able to argue that inflation will return to target without raising interest rates this month, Mendes says. (Robb Stewart, robb.stewart@wsj.com)

 

While France’s fiscal crisis is likely to get worse before it gets better, the risk of contagion appears limited, Andrew Kenningham at Capital Economics says in a note. Exposure of French corporates and banks to sovereign bonds is relatively small, decreasing the chances of a domestic doom loop, he says. “Second, in contrast to the early 2010s, the ECB is now well placed to limit contagion,” he says, noting its potential for bond or asset purchases if needed. Meanwhile, the deficits of other countries in the eurozone—which drove contagion in the early 2010s—remain stable, while political support for exiting the eurozone has declined. While a stand-off between France and the EU over fiscal policy could drive up spreads, an acute crisis remains a tail risk, Kenningham says. (Don Forbes, don.forbes@wsj.com)
